name: SPHEREx
desc:
The Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx) mission is a near-infrared all-sky spectral survey designed to: (1) map the three-dimensional large-scale distribution of galaxies to probe the origin and fate of the universe and to constrain the physics of inflation; (2) survey areas in the early stages of star and planet formation for water and organic molecules; and, (3) study the origin and history galaxy formation by tracing the total light emitted over cosmic time.

The SPHEREx satellite carries a triple mirror telescope with an effective aperture of 20 cm, a field of view of 3.5 x 11.3 degrees, and a focal length of 60 cm. The focal plane is imaged simultaneously by two mosaics of three 2k x 2k HgCdTe detector arrays separated by a dichroic beam splitter. A set of linear variable filters is placed above each detector to effectively serve as bandpass filters. The spectra cover two wavelength ranges for every 6.2-arcsecond pixel over the entire sky: 750-4100 nm at a spectral resolution of R = 40; and 4100-4800 nm at R = 150. Three V-groove radiators passively cool the entire telescope below 80K, and an additional stage of radiative cooling reduces the long wavelength focal plane temperature below 60K.

SPHEREx will be placed in a 700-km low-Earth sun-synchronous orbit, with the spacecraft pointing approximately 90 degrees from the Sun so that observations follow along a great circle that includes the north and south ecliptic planes. This orientation enables the spacecraft to produce a full sky coverage every six months during its nominal two-year mission.

The total lifecycle cost to develop, launch, and operate SPHEREx was approximately $488 million.

name: TRACERS-A
op: University of Iowa Department of Physics and Astronomy
short: NASA heliophysics spacecraft investigating solar particles interacting with Earth's magnetosphere

name: TRACERS-B
op: University of Iowa Department of Physics and Astronomy
short: NASA heliophysics spacecraft investigating solar particles interacting with Earth's magnetosphere
desc:
TRACERS-A is one of a pair of simultaneously launched satellites. TRACERS is a dual spacecraft project designed to observe fields and particles at the magnetic cusp region encircling the Earth’s north pole. During the planned 12-month primary mission, the TRACERS duo will repeatedly transit the cusp, a region in space located near the north and south poles of Earth, where magnetic field lines act as a guide for solar particles to funnel through and collide with atmospheric gases. These satellites were built by Millennium Space Systems.

The primary scientific mission objectives are to determine: (1) whether magnetopause reconnection is primarily spatially or temporally variable for a range of solar wind conditions; (2) how the reconnection rate evolves for temporally varying reconnection; and (3) to what extent dynamic structures in the cusp are associated with temporal versus spatial reconnection.

The two spacecraft carry a suite of five identical primary instruments: (1) a high-cadence fluxgate magnetometer (MAG) to measure of the background magnetic field up to 5 Hz; (2) a three-axis search coil magnetometer (MSC) to measure the AC magnetic field from 2 Hz up to 1 kHz; (3) two-axis electric field instrument (EFI) to measure electric fields at low frequencies from 0 Hz to 1 kHz and high frequencies from 0.3 MHz to 5 MHz; (4) an electrostatic analyzer for cusp electrons (ACE) to measure cusp electrons from 40 eV to 10 keV with a temporal resolution less than 100 ms over a 210-deg plane of electron directions; and (5) an analyzer for cusp ions (ACI) to measure cusp ions from 50 eV to 10 keV with a temporal resolution less than 500 ms over a 180-deg plane of ion directions. An additional experiment is Magnetometers for Innovation and Capability (MAGIC), which consists of prototype magnetic field instruments that will be tested as a technology demonstration.

The spacecraft will travel in tandem, one trailing slightly behind the other, in a circular Sun-synchronous orbit at an altitude of 590 km, with a degree of separation ranging from 75 to 900 km. They are expected to have more than 3250 encounters with the cusps in the one-year mission lifetime.

TRACERS will study magnetic reconnection and answer longstanding questions about what occurs at the magnetopause, the boundary between Earth’s magnetosphere and the solar wind. The data gathered will help to better forecast and prepare for impacts of space weather events.

name: Bard
short: microsatellite developed by York Space Systems
desc:
The Polylingual Experimental Terminal (PExT) demonstrator is managed by NASA’s Space Communications and Navigation (SCaN) program. Also known as “Bard,” the spacecraft will test an advanced communications terminal designed to enable real-time interaction between various government and commercial satellite relay networks. This is the first-of-its-kind capability.

For almost 40 years, NASA has relied on its own satellite system to provide communication links between the ground and satellites in near-Earth orbit, but NASA’s current infrastructure was not originally designed for interoperability between government and commercial networks. NASA is working with industry to develop wideband terminal technology, designed to provide interoperability to spacecraft, meaning they will be able to “roam” between government and commercial networks in space for the very first time.

The PExT payload, equipped with a compact two-foot antenna, will communicate across NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay Satellites fleet and two commercial networks. After the flight demonstration, NASA will continue to work with private industry and emerging missions to develop wideband terminal technology for the agency. NASA missions will transition to commercial communications services as early as 2028.¿

PExT was launched as part of the TRACERS mission along with TRACER A, TRACER B, EPIC, SKYKRAFT 4, LIDE, and REAL.

name: SpaceX CRS-33
short: 2025 cargo resupply mission to the International Space Station
desc:
Dragon CRS 33 is a Commercial Resupply Service mission to the International Space Station. The mission is contracted by NASA and will be flown by SpaceX using a Cargo Dragon C211. While docked, Dragon will perform a series of burns to help the International Space Station maintain its current altitude, using an independent propellant system and two Draco engines in the spacecraft’s modified trunk.

The rocket took a northeast trajectory to launch Dragon CRS 33 to the ISS, which uses a low-Earth orbit inclined 51.6 degrees to the Equator. The booster, B1090-7, was recovered on A Shortfall of Gravitas in the Atlantic Ocean.

Dragon CRS 33 will use a trunk capable of performing reboost burns of the Station, and will also carry more than 2,200 kg of supplies and experiments to ISS. Experiments that will be flown on board include one to study engineered liver tissue, effects of microgravity on bone marrow stem cells, and an orbital data center experiment involving a Red Hat Device Edge platform. Packed aboard the Dragon was enough hardware to support more than 50 science experiments and technology demonstrations, including 3D metal printing.

Dragon CRS 33 will remain docked to the space station for nearly five months, marking SpaceX’s first, long-duration cargo mission. The main reason for this is to allow the Dragon to perform multiple orbital reboosts of the ISS, keeping it in its desired position. The eventual demise of the station will be around 2030.

This is SpaceX’s 546th mission and Flacon 9’s 521st mission.

name: Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe
op: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (United States)
desc:
The Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP) is a Solar Terrestrial Probes Program mission within NASA's Heliophysics Division. IMAP is designed to resolve two major questions of heliophysics: the acceleration of energetic particles, and the interaction of the solar wind with the local interstellar medium.

The primary scientific objectives are to advance understanding of: (1) the temporal and spatial evolution of the boundary region in which the solar wind and the interstellar medium interact; (2) the processes related to the interactions of the magnetic field of the Sun and the local interstellar medium; (3) the composition and properties of the local interstellar medium; and (4) the processes related to particle injection and acceleration near the Sun and in the heliosphere and heliosheath. To achieve these goals, IMAP will measure interstellar neutral atoms (ISNs) and energetic neutral atoms (ENAs), charged particles (ions and electrons), solar wind magnetic field, interstellar dust, and ultraviolet light from inflowing interstellar H and He.

The spacecraft is a spin-stabilized, 4-rpm, sun-pointing observatory, about 2 m in diameter and 0.7 m tall, in orbit about the L1 Sun-Earth Lagrange point. The spin axis will be re-pointed daily toward the incoming solar wind. A body-mounted solar array provides power. Medium and low-gain antennas provide communications. IMAP carries ten science instruments that run continuously as the spacecraft spins.

IMAP-Lo is a single-pixel neutral atom imager that provides energy and angle-resolved measurements of ISNs (H, He, O, Ne, and D) in the energy range 0.4 - 15.6 keV at a 4 deg angular resolution, tracked over more than 180 deg in ecliptic longitude, and energy-resolved global maps of ENAs (H and O). IMAP-Lo is mounted on a pivot platform.

IMAP-Hi consists of two identical single-pixel ENA imagers that measure H, He, and heavier ENAs from the outer heliosphere in the energy range 0.4 - 15.6 keV at a 4 deg angular resolution. The two IMAP-Hi imagers are mounted 90 deg and 45 deg antisunward relative to the spacecraft spin axis.

IMAP-Ultra consists of two identical ENA imagers that utilize extended pinhole optics to image the emission of ENAs produced in the heliosheath and beyond, primarily H atoms in the energy range of about 3 - 300 keV. IMAP-Ultra is also sensitive to contributions from He and O.

The IMAP magnetometer (MAG) consists of a pair of identical triaxial fluxgate sensors that measure the solar wind at 2 Hz (128 Hz intervals) with a 10 pT resolution. Both sensors are mounted on a 2.5-m boom, one on the end and the other in an intermediate position. MAG will also stream measurements for the IMAP Active Link for Real-Time (I-ALiRT) space weather monitoring service.

Solar Wind Electron (SWE) instrument consists of a spherical selection electrostatic analyzer with seven charge electron multiplier detectors that measure the 3-D distribution of solar wind thermal and suprathermal electrons in the energy range 1 eV-5 keV at a 15-s resolution.

Solar Wind And Pickup Ion (SWAPI) instrument measures solar wind (H+ and He++) and interstellar pickup ions (He+ and H+) in the energy range 0.1-20 keV/q at a 15-s resolution. SWAPI consists of a sun-facing aperture grid, a spherical selection electrostatic analyzer, and a coincidence detector comprised of two change electron multipliers.

The Compact Dual Ion Composition Experiment (CoDICE) combines an electrostatic analyzer with a time-of-flight versus energy subsystem to simultaneously measure the 3-D velocity distribution functions, ionic charge state, and mass composition of interstellar pickup ions and solar wind ions including suprathermal particles from the Sun. The CoDICE-Lo channel measures ions in the energy range of 0.5-80 keV/q. The CoDICE-Hi channel measures arrival direction of 0.03-5 MeV/nuc ions. CoDICE-Hi also measures 20-400 keV electrons.

The High-energy Ion Telescope (HIT) is a dE/dx (energy loss) versus E (total energy) spectrometer that measures the elemental composition, energy spectra, angular distributions, and arrival times of high-energy H to Ni ions over an energy range of about 2-40 MeV/nuc. Two of the 16 silicon solid-state detectors are sensitive to high-energy electrons of about 0.5- 1.0 MeV and report these measurements to I-ALiRT.

The Interstellar Dust Experiment (IDEX) is a high-resolution time-of-flight dust impact ionization mass spectrometer that provides the elemental composition, speed, and mass distributions of interstellar dust particles from 1 to 500 amu with a mass resolution m/dm of a least 200.

GLObal solar Wind Structure (GLOWS) instrument is a non-imaging single-pixel ultraviolet Lyman-alpha photometer that measures the heliospheric backscatter ultraviolet glow from inflowing interstellar H (Lyman-alpha at 121.6 nm) and He (at 58.4 nm). GLOWS consists of two separate detectors, LaD and HeD, for the two spectral channels.

To enable continuous observations between the Sun and Earth and outside the Earth's magnetosphere, IMAP was placed in a controlled Lissajous orbit about the L1 Sun-Earth Lagrange point. The nominal mission lifetime is two years. The spacecraft has consumables for at least five years.

Falcon booster B1096 supported this mission, flying for the second time after previously launching the KF-01 mission for Amazon’s Kuiper internet constellation in July. After flying due east out of the Cape, B1096 reentered Earth’s atmosphere, performed an entry burn to slow its descent, and finally landed safely atop one of SpaceX’s east coast droneships, Just Read the Instructions, which was stationed downrange in the Atlantic Ocean.

Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP) was simultaneously launched with the Space Weather Follow On-Lagrange 1 (SWFO-L1) and the Carruthers Geocorona Observatory. This launch marked the 121st Falcon 9 mission of 2025, and the 539th overall. Furthermore, this launch was the 220th orbital launch attempt worldwide in 2025.

alt: Global Lyman-alpha Imagers of the Dynamic Exosphere (GLIDE)
desc:
The Carruthers Geocorona Observatory (CGO), formerly known as the Global Lyman-alpha Imagers of the Dynamic Exosphere (GLIDE), is a Solar Terrestrial Probes Program mission within NASA's Heliophysics Division. The spacecraft is designed to acquire high-resolution, wide-field images of the far ultraviolet light emitted by hydrogen atoms in the Earth's exosphere. The primary scientific objectives are to: (1) study the nature and origins of the global 3-D structure of the Earth's exosphere and its temporal variability; and (2) improve understanding of how exosphere interacts with and recovers from space weather events. It is the first mission dedicated to continuous observation of and tracking changes in the exosphere.

The spacecraft is a small space telescope that carries far ultraviolet imagers equipped with filters for observing in the wavelength range of 100-200 nm, including Lyman-alpha emission. A solar array panel, consisting of high-efficiency, radiation-hardened, quadruple-junction solar cells, provides power.

Falcon booster B1096 supported this mission, flying for the second time after previously launching the KF-01 mission for Amazon’s Kuiper internet constellation in July. After flying due east out of the Cape, B1096 reentered Earth’s atmosphere, performed an entry burn to slow its descent, and finally landed safely atop one of SpaceX’s east coast droneships, Just Read the Instructions, which was stationed downrange in the Atlantic Ocean.

Carruthers Geocorona Observatory was simultaneously launched with IMAP and the Space Weather Follow On-Lagrange 1 (SWFO-L1). This launch marked the 121st Falcon 9 mission of 2025, and the 539th overall. Furthermore, this launch was the 220th orbital launch attempt worldwide in 2025.

To enable continuous, unobstructed imaging of the exosphere, the spacecraft will be placed in an orbit about the L1 Sun-Earth Lagrange point, 1.5 million km toward the Sun. The nominal mission lifetime is two years.

name: EscaPADE Blue
alt: Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorer Blue
short: spacecraft designed to conduct heliophysics research in orbit of Mars
desc:
The Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (EscaPADE) are a dual-spacecraft mission to study ion and sputtered escape from Mars. The planned launch on the Blue Origin New Glenn booster from Cape Canaveral, originally scheduled for October 13, 2024, has been delayed indefinitely. The science goals of the mission are to: understand the processes controlling the structure of Mars' hybrid magnetosphere and how it guides ion flows; understand how energy and momentum are transported from the solar wind through Mars' magnetosphere; and understand the processes controlling the flow of energy and matter into and out of the collisional atmosphere. EscaPADE is part of the NASA Small Innovative Missions for Planetary Exploration (SIMPLEx) program.

## Spacecraft and Subsystems

Each identical EscaPADE spacecraft (named "Blue" and "Gold") has a dry mass of 209 kg, and a fully fueled mass of 535 kg. The spacecraft (using a Rocket Lab Photon bus) is 4.88 x 1.65 x 1.09 m. The spacecraft is powered by four (two pairs) fixed solar panel wings extending from opposite sides of the spacecraft, which can generate 288 W at Mars aphelion. The science payload requires approximately 128 W. The arrays charge a 7s5p battery assembly. Main engine propulsion is provided by hypergolic bipropellant monoxides of nitrogen (MON) and monomethyl hydrazine (MMH). Cold nitrogen gas thrusters and four reaction wheels are used to maintain orientation. Ten tanks are mounted in the spacecraft, two for fuel, two for oxidizer, two for the helium pressurant, and four for the nitrogen. Orientation knowledge is provided by two star trackers and four fine Sun sensors. Communications are in X-band via a 60 cm diameter radial line slot array high-gain dish antenna. There are also four low-gain and two medium gain patch antennas mounted on the spacecraft. A 2 meter long boom extends from the spacecraft holding some of the science instruments, and the main engine nozzle extends from the bottom.

There are three science experiments onboard each spacecraft, EMAG, EESA, and ELP. EMAG is a magnetometer that will measure DC magnetic fields up to 1000 nT, mounted at the end and partway up the boom. EESA is an electrostatic analyzer designed to measure suprathermal ions from 2 eV to 20 keV and suprathermal electrons from 3 eV to 10 keV. It is mounted on the upper deck of the spacecraft bus. ELP is a Langmuir probe measuring plasma density from 20 - 30,000 particles per cubic cm and solar EUV flux from 5 - 20 milliwatts per square meter, and is mounted on the boom and on the spacecraft bus.

## Mission Profile

The launch has been delayed indefinitely. The details of the new launch, cruise, and orbital plan will be changed, although the science plan should be similar. For reference, the original plan, with a launch in October, 2024, was as follows:

After launch from Cape Canaveral on a Blue Origin New Glenn launch vehicle, EscaPADE would have gone into a 1.6 day elliptical Earth orbit, followed by a trans-Mars injection and a direct ballistic Hohmann Type II transfer orbit. The 11 month trajectory would reach Mars and go into a highly elliptical orbit in September 2025. Over roughly 7 months the orbits were to be adjusted until they reached the nominal science orbits in April 2026. The initial science campaign involved both spacecraft flying in the same orbit, 160 x 8400 km altitude with an inclination of 60 degrees. This would last approximately 6 months, at which time one of the spacecraft would go into an orbit which "crosses" the orbit of the other spacecraft, both still with 160 km periapses, one with an apoapse of 7000 km and one at 10,000 km. This campaign would operate for approximately 5 months. End of primary science mission and close-out was planned for March 2027.

name: Sentinel-6B
desc:
Sentinel-6B is a joint US-European ocean monitoring satellite. It is the second of two Jason Continuity of Service (Jason-CS) missions, launching five years after its sister satellite, Sentinel-6A Michael Freilich. The Sentinel-6 satellites are the current generation in a long-running series of ocean topography satellites.

The mission is a collaborative effort between space and environmental agencies on both sides of the Atlantic. The European Organization for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (EUMETSAT) will operate the satellite in partnership with the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA), and the distinct European Union Space Program also have roles within the project.

Sentinel-6B is part of Copernicus, the European Union’s Earth observation program. It uses a constellation of satellites with differing instruments and capabilities to build a detailed picture of our planet and its environment. Sentinel-6’s specific role is to measure global sea levels, wave heights, and ocean winds.

The Sentinel-6B satellite has a mass of 1,190 kg, measuring 5.8 m in length, 2.4 m in height, and 4.3 m in width in a deployed configuration with its solar panels extended. It will operate in a low-Earth orbit (LEO) with an inclination of 66 degrees, an average of 1,336 km above the surface. From this orbit, it will be able to observe 95% of Earth’s oceans that are not covered with ice, repeating its track every 10 days.

Sentinel-6B has the same suite of instruments as Sentinel-6A. Its primary scientific payload is Poseidon 4, a radar altimeter featuring a 1.2-meter parabolic reflector. Poseidon 4 transmits a pulse of radio waves toward the Earth’s surface and records how long it takes for the signal to reflect back. This enables precise calculation of the distance between the satellite and the ocean surface. When combined with the spacecraft’s orbital parameters, the height of the ocean surface can be measured.

Poseidon-4 uses both conventional pulse-width and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) techniques to collect data. It uses two radio frequencies, with its primary observations using a Ku-band frequency centered around 13.575 GHz. Secondary observations are made using a C-band frequency centered around 5.41 GHz to correct for interference in the ionosphere, and to make additional measurements of sea state and rain cells in the atmosphere. As well as ranging, Poseidon provides a radar cross-section for deriving wave height and wind speeds.

The Advanced Microwave Radiometer for Climate (AMR-C) measures radiation reflected from the ocean surface to monitor water vapor content in the atmosphere that might affect Poseidon-4’s readings, allowing an appropriate correction to be made to its data. AMR-C consists of two radiometers. The core AMR instrument measures the brightness temperature at three different frequencies: 18.7, 23.8, and 34 GHz, following on from similar instruments on previous-generation satellites.

It is key to Sentinel-6B’s mission that the satellite’s exact position in space is known at the point it takes each of its readings. To achieve this, the spacecraft carries the Precise Orbit Determination (POD) package, a suite of instruments dedicated to measuring the parameters of its orbit. This includes Doppler Orbitography and Radiopositioning Integrated by Satellite (DORIS) DGXX-SEV, which uses the Doppler shift of signals from a network of 55 ground-based beacons around the world to determine its velocity relative to those points on the surface.

The Global Navigation Satellite System Precise Orbit Determination (GNSS-POD) package uses a pair of receivers — one active and a cold spare — to determine the satellite’s position from navigation satellite signals. A Laser Retroreflector array is also part of the POD package to support ground-based measurements.

As well as using satellite navigation signals to determine its orbit, Sentinel-6B will use these signals and the way they interact with the Earth’s atmosphere to measure atmospheric properties. Global Navigation Satellite System Radio Occultation (GNSS-RO) payload uses two additional antennae to the one used by GNSS-POD to track signals from satellites close to the limb of the Earth — the horizon as seen from the satellite — with one antenna pointing forward and the other behind the satellite. The satellite studies how the signals are refracted as they pass through the atmosphere to build a profile of temperature, pressure, and water content.

Airbus Defence and Space was the prime contractor for the satellite, which was built in Friedrichshafen, Germany. The satellite had been kept in storage under carefully-controlled conditions since construction and initial testing were completed in 2022. This was Falcon 9’s 565th mission and SpaceX’s 592nd mission.

name: SpaceX CRS-34
short: 2026 cargo resupply mission to the International Space Station
desc:
SpaceX CRS-34 is a Commercial Resupply Service mission to the International Space Station. The mission is contracted by NASA and will be flown by SpaceX using a Cargo Dragon.

Cargo Dragon C209 was launched into a 51.6-degree orbit to match the International Space Station’s (ISS) orbit, and the cargo ship will take roughly 38 hours to reach ISS. It will dock to the Harmony module’s forward port.

Cargo Dragon is carrying around 2,948 kg of supplies to the ISS, including a variety of food, equipment, and experiments. There have been more than 4,000 experiments aboard the Station over its 25 year lifespan, conducted by scientists from 110 countries, and there are 831 kg of experiments aboard.

The Outcomes of microbial Dynamics during Spaceflight and in SimulatEd microgravity (ODYSSEY) experiment is designed to test the fidelity of microgravity simulators on Earth by comparing them to actual behavior of two species of bacteria in space. ODYSSEY will evaluate biofilm formation and exchange of genetic material in bacteria in the microgravity environment.

The Storm Time O+ Ring current Imaging Evolution (STORIE) will investigate a captive swarm of charged particles trapped in Earth’s donut-shaped ring current that is sandwiched between the two Van Allen belts and is part of Earth’s magnetic field. STORIE is flying as part of the U.S. Space Force’s Space Test Program-Houston 11 (STP-H11) payload and will be installed on the exterior of ISS by the Canadarm2 a few days after its arrival.

Laplace is an experiment designed to study how dust particles behave in space, in particular, how these particles aggregate. This experiment also examines how particles and gas move in dust clouds in microgravity, and researchers hope to better understand how clouds of dust and gas can form planets and solar systems.

The Green Bone in Microgravity experiment is designed to grow human bone cells on a biomimetic rattan wood scaffold known as b.Bone aboard the Station. Microgravity causes bone loss in humans similar to that caused by osteoporosis, and scientists hope to test this bone scaffold’s performance under similar conditions. Scaffolds can be used to help repair weak bones.

Spleen Activity in Space Anemia and Red Cells Kinetics (SPARK) uses ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging to study how the spleen changes in microgravity. SPARK also measures how red blood cells break down and looks for hemolysis markers. Anemia has been noted in astronauts returning from space, and it is important to avoid serious anemia during long-duration missions to the Moon or Mars.

The CLARREO Pathfinder, which will be mounted on an external platform on the Station’s truss, is designed to accurately measure sunlight reflected off Earth and to help calibrate other on-orbit sensors that monitor solar reflectivity. These measurements can improve our understanding of how sensitive Earth is to greenhouse gas emissions.

Also mounted on the STP-H11 external payload, which will be mounted on the Columbus laboratory module, is the Autonomous Ion Mass Spectrometer Sentry (AIMSS) experiment. AIMSS is designed to measure ionospheric plasma in high resolution, as well as to measure the thruster plumes of visiting vehicles and the effects on that plasma.

These experiments are joined by others as well as 618 kg of crew supplies, 128 kg of spacewalk equipment, 469 kg of vehicle hardware, 84 kg of computer resources, and 816 kg of unpressurized payloads. Among other things, a replacement power cable for a European exercise device, an on-orbit spare catalytic reactor for the water management system, and a pretreatment concentrate tank for the Station’s toilets are also onboard the Cargo Dragon.

NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway and European Space Agency (ESA) astronaut Sophie Adenot will monitor Dragon’s arrival. After it docks, the Cargo Dragon will spend about a month docked to the ISS before leaving the Station in mid-June and returning to Earth with cargo. It will splashdown in the Pacific with time-critical experiment samples and hardware to be returned for repair, or in the case of the Advanced Plant Habitat, eventual museum display.

The rocket for this mission, Falcon 9, is a 3.9 m diameter, 70 m tall two-stage rocket. Falcon booster B1096, flying on its sixth mission, launched on a northeast trajectory and conducted a successful return-to-launch-site with a landing at Landing Zone 40 (LZ-40), located directly adjacent to SLC-40.

This was Falcon 9’s 639th mission, Space X’s 667th mission, and the 112th orbital launch attempt of 2026.

name: SpaceX Crew-13
short: 2026 American crewed spaceflight to the ISS
desc:
SpaceX Crew-13 is the thirteenth operational crewed rotation mission of a Crew Dragon spacecraft to the International Space Station under the Commercial Crew Program, Crew-13. The crew is composed of NASA astronauts commander Jessica Watkins and pilot Luke Delaney, and mission specialists Joshua Kutryk of CSA and Sergey Teteryatnikov of Russia's Roscosmos.

Once settled into life aboard the Station, the four crew members will begin conducting research, science experiments, and Station maintenance procedures. During their six-month stay, the SpaceX Crew-13 astronauts are conducting hundreds of scientific investigations. Key experiments focus on human health, space manufacturing, and deep-space mission readiness:

Venous Haemostasis: A collaborative study between NASA and ESA using MRI, ultrasounds, and blood tracking to understand blood flow abnormalities and clot risks in microgravity.

B-Complex: Evaluates the effectiveness of B-vitamin supplements in preventing Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), which causes vision changes in astronauts.

RelaxPro & Health Tracking: Uses smartwatches and health monitoring sensors to log sleep, track health data, and evaluate relaxation techniques for deep-space missions. Stem Cell-Derived Tissues: Producing human stem cell-derived tissues in microgravity to improve disease modeling, drug testing, and treatments for Parkinson's disease and heart disease.

Cartilage Bioprinting: Utilizing the Auxilium bioprinter to print high-quality cartilage tissue samples, which form better in weightlessness than on Earth. MIYOKA (Lead-Free Soldering): Testing techniques for safe electronics manufacturing and repair in space to reduce reliance on ground-support supply missions.

Manual Piloting Simulations: Testing astronauts' ability to manually control spacecraft during lunar-landing simulations after long exposure to microgravity. Autonomous Crop Production: Growing fresh produce using mostly autonomous plant growth facilities and plant pillows scattered throughout the station to sustain future crews on Mars and Moon journeys. Zero T2: Tracking exercise metrics on specialized treadmills to evaluate the physical strain limits of deep-space voyages.

The rocket body for this mission, Falcon 9, is a two-stage medium-lift launch vehicle. It stands 69.8 m tall and 3.7 m wide. The reusable first stage booster features nine Merlin engines that produce 7,600 kilonewtons (kN) of thrust at liftoff. The first stage booster also features four landing legs and four grid fins for recovery. The Falcon 9 second stage features a single, vacuum-optimized Merlin engine that produces 934 kN of thrust. Both stages utilize liquid oxygen (LOX) and highly refined kerosene (RP-1) as propellants. Falcon 9 booster B1101 supported this mission.

This is Falcon 9’s 692nd mission, SpaceX’s 724th mission, and the 234th orbital launch attempt of 2026.

name: SpaceX CRS-35
short: 2026 cargo resupply mission to the International Space Station
desc:
SpaceX CRS-35 (Cargo Dragon C211) is a Commercial Resupply Service mission to the International Space Station. The mission was contracted by NASA and flown by SpaceX using a Cargo Dragon. Most notably, this mission will deliver the fourth pair of iROSA solar arrays which will be used to provide additional power to the station. CRS-35 took a northeast trajectory after liftoff, placing the Cargo Dragon in an orbit inclined 51.6 degrees to the equator, the same inclination used by the Station.

CRS-35 is carrying 2,867 kg of cargo to the Station. This includes 593 kg of science experiments, 383 kg of crew supplies, 362 kg of vehicle hardware, 189 kg of spacewalk equipment, and 36 kg of computer resources. Additionally, it is carrying 1,195 kg of cargo in its unpressurized trunk.

The unpressurized cargo in the trunk is the last set of Redwire-developed, Boeing-contracted iROSA solar arrays to augment the Station’s power supply. These final arrays will be installed on power channel 3B on the starboard S6 truss segment and on channel 2A on the port P4 truss segment. Six iROSA arrays, each generating 20 to 28 kilowatts of electricity, are already installed on the ISS. Once these final arrays are attached during future spacewalks, the Station will receive an additional 20 to 30% of power. This will improve the power supply margin to keep the ISS going through its final years and decommissioning, as the original solar arrays that launched with the Station are aging and degraded.

The 593 kg of science experiments include studies of vision, heart tissue, glass making, and neurodegenerative diseases. One notable experiment is the LambdaVision-1, which will test manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity. The experiment will manufacture these retinas one thin layer at a time, and investigators hope that the microgravity environment will enable more uniform, stable layers, improving the retinas’ performance.

The Stellar Spheroids experiment will study how the microgravity environment affects growth and function of 3D human heart tissue models. Investigators will test whether microgravity can lead to more advanced vascular networks, with potential outcomes including more realistic heart tissue models to support disease research and larger-scale drug testing.

Another experiment, ELF-Unconventional Glass 2, will form glass in microgravity using non-traditional elements. Behavior of molten material will be studied, and solid samples will be returned to Earth. Investigators hope this will lead to stronger, more durable, and more capable glass for spacecraft and other technologies.

Additionally, the MINDS experiment will study brain organoids in “organoid villages” combining cells from multiple people. This study is meant to better understand inflammation that can lead to neurodegenerative diseases. Investigators hope to identify new treatment targets for Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis.

The Cargo Dragon will spend around a month in orbit before returning to Earth off the coast of California with critical samples and other cargo. It’s ability to return cargo to Earth is critical for maintaining the Station’s Shuttle-era extravehicular mobility unit spacesuits, as well as other ISS systems. CRS-35 will return one spacesuit to Earth for refurbishment, and the spacecraft will also return a urine processor pump assembly and a water processor filtration unit.

The rocket for this mission, Falcon 9, is a 3.9 m diameter, 70 m tall two-stage rocket. Falcon booster B1096, flying on its eighth mission, launched on a northeast trajectory and conducted a successful return-to-launch-site with a landing at Landing Zone 40 (LZ-40), located directly adjacent to SLC-40.

This was Falcon 9’s 696th mission, Space X’s 729th mission, and the 241st orbital launch attempt of 2026.
